articles.text: LNU, SCU, CZU Lightning Complex fires have burned over 800,000 acres On August 17, lightning strikes started hundreds of fires across Northern California. In the days since, over one million acres have burned. California is currently under a state of emergency, and all Cal Fire resources are overextended in battling these fires. Since they broke out a week ago, three of the largest wildfire complexes (LNU, SCU, and CZU) have burned over 800,000 acres combined, and have destroyed 1,000 structures as of press time. Two of the complexes have already ranked as the second and third largest in California history. The complexes encircle the San Francisco Bay Area in Napa and Sonoma counties (LNU complex), Santa Cruz county (CZU complex), and Santa Clara, Alameda, Contra Costa, San Joaquin and Stanislaus counties (SCU complex). The complexes are named with acronyms to indicate geographical locators based on Cal Fire administrative unit codes. LNU, for example, designates the areas that are part of the Sonoma-Lake-Napa unit, comprising Sonoma, Lake, Napa, Colusa, Solano, and Yolo counties. Fires managed by that unit are grouped under that prefix. SCU refers to the areas that are administratively under the Cal Fire SCU unit – Santa Clara, Alameda, Contra Costa, San Joaquin and Stanislaus counties. CZU refers to the San Mateo-Santa Cruz unit. Piedmont Fire Engine 2880 was deployed after 9 p.m. on Friday night, August 21, for an “immediate need” assignment as part of a local Task Force assigned to the SCU Lightning Complex. The three-man crew is led by Lt. Justin McNulty, with engineers Russ San Fillippo and Justin Morris. “Piedmont Fire Department immediately accepted the call for assistance,” said Fire Chief Bret Black. The SCU Lightning Complex has burned the most acres of the three, making it the second largest wildfire in state history. The majority of the destruction has been limited to Stanislaus and San Joaquin counties. As of press time, it had burned 360,055 acres, with 15 percent containment as of Tuesday morning, August 25. Joining the Piedmont firefighters on the task force are firefighters from Hayward, Alameda, East Bay Regional Parks and San Mateo departments. Black added that the fire is not a threat to Piedmont. The CZU Lightning Complex, the smallest of the three fires, is also the least contained. It had burned 78,869 acres and was 17 percent contained on Wednesday morning. One Santa Cruz county man died and seven others have been reported missing, and 330 structures have been destroyed. The LNU Lightning Complex is, thus far, the deadliest and most destructive of the three fires in terms of structure damage. It has burned 352,913 acres and was 27 percent contained as of Tuesday morning. Five people died in Napa and Sonoma counties, and 1,188 total structures have been damaged or destroyed.

articles.text: No new cases of COVID-19 were reported amongst Piedmonters over the past seven days, but the number of positive cases in Alameda County continued to grow. As of yesterday, August 25, the number is 16,738 according to the Alameda County Public Health Department. This represents a 12 percent increase. Health officials reported 10 more deaths since last Tuesday, August 18, bringing the total number of fatalities due to COVID-19 to 234 in Alameda County. Six cases were reported in Piedmont earlier in August and the total number of cases for the City stands at 29. Earlier in the month, officials said that an electronic reporting issue was resolved and this resulted in a sudden uptick in cases. However, some of the newly reported cases due to the repaired process come from early in the year, and it is not clear if the new Piedmont cases are all from August or were from prior months. Oakland, the most populous city in the county, now has 6,866 cases. Hayward counted 2,357 cases and Fremont has 1,120. The state still has Alameda County on a COVID-19 “watchlist” along with most other counties in California. Alameda County has been on the list since July 12, meaning many indoor businesses and activities are prohibited by state regulations. On Friday, August 21, county officials allowed some new sectors of the economy to reopen for the first time in weeks. Outdoor public pools are now allowed to open as long as they follow protocols, as well as some personal services, like barbers, nail salons and non-medical massages, but the business has to be conducted completely outdoors.

A man sat at a metro station in Washington DC and started to play the violin; it was a cold January morning. He played six Bach pieces for about 45 minutes. During that time, since it was rush hour, it was calculated that thousands of people went through the station, most of them on their way to work. Three minutes went by and a middle-aged man noticed there was a musician playing. He slowed his pace and stopped for a few seconds and then hurried up to meet his schedule. A minute later, the violinist received his first dollar tip: a woman threw the money in the till and without stopping continued to walk. A few minutes later, someone leaned against the wall to listen to him, but the man looked at his watch and started to walk again. Clearly, he was late for work. The one who paid the most attention was a 3-year-old boy. His mother tugged him along, but the child stopped to look at the violinist. articles.text: Editor: Jen Cavenaugh is a true gift to the Piedmont community and has been an outstanding member of our city council. Her contributions to the council and our city have been numerous and exemplary. There is no question in my mind that Jen should be reelected to our city council. Jen approaches opportunities in the way that you would expect of a University of Chicago MBA, Accenture (Andersen Consulting) executive, and Clorox manager. She identifies opportunities, analyzes them, develops solutions, connects with people, enlists them in the efforts, manages the processes, and gets results. My first exposure to Jen and her work was a community research plan she did in 2014 for the Recreation Commission as a volunteer consultant. It defined Piedmont community recreational interests, priorities, and unmet needs. It was an outstanding, highly professional report that inspired me. Since that first exposure to Jen, I have been constantly amazed by the breath of her interests, her energy, her desire to take on new challenges, and make Piedmont better. But this is what she just naturally does. Jen Cavenaugh is a force that Piedmont needs, and I am thankful we have her. I strongly support and recommend Jen’s reelection to the Piedmont City Council. –Dick Carter of the city council. She is honest, direct, compassionate, and a good listener. One aspect of Jen that I find particularly engaging--and is such a gift for our city--is that she is always pressing forward. She doesn’t dwell on past decisions or judge others; she continually works to identify needs and consider solutions, to reach out to others to gain information or spread the word. Whether there is a community need or celebration, she shows up. She doesn’t hesitate to do the hard work or cast an unpopular vote to support what she believes is best for Piedmont. Jen has a quick mind, strong business acumen, and a deep knowledge of Piedmont. She respects our history while recognizing areas of needed improvement, and understands how to use our limited resources and prioritize our most critical issues. Please join me in voting to reelect Jen Cavenaugh for Piedmont City Council in November. Sincerely, –Megan Pillsbury Piedmont Board of Education
articles.title: Jen Cavenaugh – working to make Piedmont better

Sincerely, –Megan Pillsbury Piedmont Board of Education Leaf-blowers are greenhouse gas polluters Editor: Curiously, the city’s proposed REACH codes make no attempt to reduce greenhouse gases (GHG) produced from gas-powered leaf blowers, even though the California Air Resource Board (CARB) computes that 1-hr of their operation is equivalent to 1,100 driven auto miles. City ordinance 517 N.S. banned gas powered leaf blowers in 1990 because of their noise pollution. Many proponents of the REACH codes insist that stopping climate change necessitates elimination of natural gas appliances. How about enforcing the leaf-blower ban first? That’s a GHG-reducing measure that would be music to our ears. –Dai Meagher For sake of climate, residents urged to support Reach Codes Editor: Along with 90% of our fellow Piedmonters (according to recent survey results), we worry about the world we will leave behind if we don’t take serious action to prevent the worst-case scenarios for climate change. Case in point: this week’s smoke-filled air becoming the new normal with more frequent and intense wildfires. The Reach Codes now before City Council offer a reasonable and concrete step in the right direction, by assisting our transition away from natural gas, a greenhouse gas-emitting fossil fuel that contributes to climate change. Heating our homes and water with natural gas accounts for almost half of the emissions created within Piedmont’s boundaries. We can’t move the needle on our climate goals without using less natural gas, whether through better insulating our homes and pipes, adding rooftop solar, or replacing natural gas appliances over time with new, efficient electric appliances. As many as 30 other leading California cities are adopting Reach Codes, and even PG&E supports this long-term shift away from natural gas. City staff led a thorough, year-long process to develop the Codes, incorporating a great deal of public input. In particular, staff responded to concerns about one-size-fits-all requirements by developing a menu of options for energy upgrades, based on the preferences, budget, and individual circumstances of each homeowner, including many low-cost options. The upgrades will be triggered by sizable renovations or expansions to Piedmont’s aging housing infrastructure, when it is most pragmatic and cost-effective to do so. For more details, visit https://www.piedmont.ca.gov/ government/city_news___notifications/council_consideration_ of_reach_codes_deferred. Reach Code requirements are relatively minor in the scheme of home renovations, but are important steps in tackling climate change. It would be a real shame if we shirk our collective responsibility by passing up on this opportunity. We urge our fellow residents to show that this community cares about climate action by writing to Council today (citycouncil@ piedmont.ca.gov) to support the adoption of Reach Codes. –Signed Katie Aubrecht, Indira Balkisoon, Elizabeth Behrens, Marj Blackwell, realtor Moira Chapman, Irene Cheng, Ellington Davis (PUSD alum), Jonathan Davis, Jezabel Droga (PHS student), Glenn Friedman, Amy Griffith (PUSD parent), Claudia Harrison, Toby Jacob (PHS student), Garrett Keating, Judy Kelly, Ronna Kelly, Russell Griffith (PUSD parent), Zenobia Lloyd (PHS student), Mara Lovric (PHS student), Marianne Mitosinka, George Wick, Samantha Miller, Susan Miller-Davis, Margaret Ovenden, Henri F. articles.text: Yes, there are hundreds of wildfires all over our state right now, most out of control. The biggest negative for most, surprisingly, will be mental health, I’m convinced. Apart from Santa Cruz, Vacaville and Healdsburg, these fires are mostly in remote parts with few inhabitants, few homes. But the situation is unexpectedly depressing, piled on top of other existing news: The killer Coronavirus that just won’t go away, and the related health and expense for both teachers and schools, plus the isolation it causes from friends and most relatives. And then we have a depressed economy and unemployment both real and anticipated, the instability and deadlocks in our national government, virtual schooling that forces parents to stay home and not work, the drought, our troubled foreign policy, foreign governments known to meddle in our upcoming election, and the uncertainty about the future resultant from the multiple distresses. Then too the officially “unhealthy” smoky air over so many of our cities day after day. All these negatives will be weighing on the citizenry even after long-overdue November rains wipe out the fires. Just consider the kids locked out of classrooms now for six-plus months, with brains ill-equipped to catch up. Nonetheless, my conviction is that after all these trials pass, we will all emerge stronger and more resilient than ever. Only we’re not in Nirvana any more. articles.text: Camp Smart Start is the Piedmont Recreation Department’s (PRD) response to in-person childcare during this unusual academic school year. “We’re trying to support working families and working parents by providing childcare and support for elementary school students during their distance learning,” Recreation Supervisor Jackson Stearns said. The camp is following the same model as Camp Almost Everything, that was rolled out by the recreation department this summer. Camp Smart Start consists of small cohorts of students, and “pods” are no greater than 12 children. Students are required to wear masks and socially distance themselves from one another. Daily health screenings are provided. As a three-week session, it is similar in length to Camp Almost Everything. Stearns said the biggest difference is the support given to Piedmont students in distance learning. “School staff and Recreation Department staff are working with students during the school day, making sure they log in [to class] on time to their synchronous learning classes, as well as complete their asynchronous assignments and submit those in a timely manner,” Stearns said. Currently, 57 students are enrolled, divided into six groups operating at all campsites. One group is at Wildwood Elementary, two groups are at Beach, and three groups are at Havens. There is currently a waiting list for a 2nd session. Stearns admits that the first day provided a learning curve for staff, as both students and staff became acclimated to distance learning programs. “Because this is brand new both for the district and the staff, we knew there would be some challenges just learning the computer systems. I’m happy to say that the majority of the students were able to log in successfully, complete their assignments and do the work,” Stearns said. He confirmed that he plans to work closely with the principals of the three schools. Smoke in the air from surrounding wildfires presented the camp’s “first big curveball” on Monday, Stearns acknowledged. “We did shut down the program around lunchtime, and will be closed for the foreseeable future until air conditions improve,” he said. Camp Smart Start is for students from transitional Kindergarten through grade five, and is entirely outdoors. Residents can register for the lottery based upon their child’s school assignment. All “pods” will match school district cohorts to the best of the department’s capability. The school district provides students with Chromebook laptops, and students are asked to come to camp with their laptop, charger, headphones, and stationary. “We are asking the parents to treat [this camp] as school,” Stearns said. While the camp is not to be treated as a replacement for school, staff will support both teachers and students in distance learning. Camp Smart Start staff are not teachers or tutors, but they communicate and work closely with parents to support students in their distance learning classes and assignments. For more information on the camp, visit https://piedmont. ca.gov/services___departments/ recreation/camp_smart_start.

Camp Smart Start consists of small cohorts of students, and “pods” are no greater than 12 children. Students are required to wear masks and socially distance themselves from one another. Daily health screenings are provided. As a three-week session, it is similar in length to Camp Almost Everything. Stearns said the biggest difference is the support given to Piedmont students in distance learning. “School staff and Recreation Department staff are working with students during the school day, making sure they log in [to class] on time to their synchronous learning classes, as well as complete their asynchronous assignments and submit those in a timely manner,” Stearns said. Currently, 57 students are enrolled, divided into six groups operating at all campsites. One group is at Wildwood Elementary, two groups are at Beach, and three groups are at Havens. There is currently a waiting list for a 2nd session. Stearns admits that the first day provided a learning curve for staff, as both students and staff became acclimated to distance learning programs. “Because this is brand new both for the district and the staff, we knew there would be some challenges just learning the computer systems. I’m happy to say that the majority of the students were able to log in successfully, complete their assignments and do the work,” Stearns said. He confirmed that he plans to work closely with the principals of the three schools. Smoke in the air from surrounding wildfires presented the camp’s “first big curveball” on Monday, Stearns acknowledged. “We did shut down the program around lunchtime, and will be closed for the foreseeable future until air conditions improve,” he said. Camp Smart Start is for students from transitional Kindergarten through grade five, and is entirely outdoors. Residents can register for the lottery based upon their child’s school assignment. All “pods” will match school district cohorts to the best of the department’s capability. The school district provides students with Chromebook laptops, and students are asked to come to camp with their laptop, charger, headphones, and stationary. “We are asking the parents to treat [this camp] as school,” Stearns said. While the camp is not to be treated as a replacement for school, staff will support both teachers and students in distance learning. Camp Smart Start staff are not teachers or tutors, but they communicate and work closely with parents to support students in their distance learning classes and assignments. For more information on the camp, visit https://piedmont. ca.gov/services___departments/ recreation/camp_smart_start. articles.text: Like many other seasonal events across the Bay Area, this year’s Harvest Festival, originally scheduled for Piedmont Park on Sunday, September 27, will be a virtual celebration due to gathering restrictions brought on by the pandemic. “As disappointing as not having an in-person event is, the city recognizes that the most important thing right now is to keep the community safe and healthy,” said Recreation Director Chelle Putzer. “Because of the nature of the Harvest Festival, social distancing measures would not be possible to achieve, let alone enforce, during this event,” This year’s Festival will feature a photo contest and a youth coloring, drawing, and collage contest. The Recreation Department encourages Piedmont residents to share harvest gardening successes with the virtual festival. Residents and school district employees can email photos of their home-grown edibles, preserves and cooking at one photo per category. Photos may be sent directly to Putzer at cputzer@ piedmont.ca.gov. Submissions must include your name, category entered, email and home address. The deadline for photo submissions is Friday, September 18. Everyone who enters will get a participation ribbon and will be entered into a random drawing for a $60 gift certificate from Ace Grand Lake Nursery on October 5. Categories for submissions include: tomato, pumpkin, squash, jam, bread, mustard, best cookie, dried fruit and veggie, salsa, unusual fruit, curds and butters, jam, apple pie, cake, cucumber pickles, ugly edible, honey, preserved edible, “other” pie, pesto and sauce, preserved veggie, and compost pile. The youth coloring contest is sponsored by the Piedmont Garden Club. Kids ages 14 and younger can download a poster, create their own vegetable drawing or make a collage from the nature scavenger hunt page found on the recreation department’s website. E-mail a copy of the project to cputzer@piedmont. ca.gov. “[This] is essentially a way to engage all the ages as we’re all sheltering in place,” said Susan Hill, founder of the Harvest Festival. She added that designing the festival virtually allows for a wider breadth of possibilities. For more infor mation, visit https://piedmont.ca.gov/ harvestfestival. Louboutin, age 57, was born and raised a few blocks from the cultural arts museum in the working-class 12th district neighborhood. The show is tied by the cultural thread of local boy makes good, but the museum was his playground. The two schools he attended were located behind the museum and he spent countless hours dreaming of faraway travel and enmeshed in the museum’s artifacts, mosaics and sculpted arts. He was especially drawn to the impossibly brilliant-hued, 5,000 species of fish in the lower-level aquarium. The museum’s main floor houses the national colonial immigration story, a permanent exhibition spanning two centuries of peoples’ emigrating from France’s far-flung colonies in Indochina, Africa, and the South Pacific. Formally known as Palais de la Porte Dorée, the visitor entry is through an iron-fence gate leading into a broad aproned courtyard for casual food service. Mounting the stairway, one instantly marvels at the sculpted facade circling the structure. The façade’s intricacies, I determine, warrant a separate visit. articles.text: The show must go on! And so, the 107th edition of the world’s most famous cycling race, the Tour de France, is set to begin in real time on August 29 in Nice. The storied race will end on September 20 in Paris. The coronavirus pandemic forced race officials to delay the start of the race from June 27 to the end of this month. articles.text: East Bay Regional closes all of its inland parks With extreme fire activity returning to Northern California and the Bay Area, parks and other outdoor activities have been closed. East Bay Regional Parks announced this week on Monday, August 24, that all of its inland parks are officially closed. The East Bay Parks that remain open are Crown Beach in Alameda, Hayward Shoreline, MLK Shoreline I Oakland, Berkeley Marina’s McLaughlin Eastshore, San Leandro’s Oyster Bay, Point Isabel in Richmond, and Quarry Lakes in Fremont. Six East Bay Regional Parks are currently within the SCU complex; Del Valle, Mission Peak, Morgan Territory, Pleasanton Ridge, Round Valley, and Sunol. The total number of park closures is estimated at 200, the highest in history. As of Tuesday morning, 795,554 total acres surrounding the Bay Area have burned due to LNU, SCU, and CZU lightning complex fires. Three more fires have burned another 125,473 acres thus far: Tehama/Glenn Zone, River Fire, and Sheep Fire. The SCU Complex Fire hits closest to home for residents of the East Bay with the fire raging through five counties: Alameda (southern end), Contra Costa, Santa Clara, San Joaquin, and Stanislaus. Its 363,772 acres already make it the second-largest fire in state history with just 15 percent containment as of Tuesday, overtaking LNU’s 352,913 acres, the third largest, with 27 percent containment yesterday. The SCU encompasses three zones: Calaveras (Alameda, Santa Clara, Stanislaus counties), Canyon (Stanislaus, San Joaquin, Merced counties), and Deer— which has been fully contained as of Tuesday in the Morgan Territory. Nearest to Piedmont, the SCU’s northernmost burn area of the Morgan Territory Regional Preserve and Los Vaqueros Reservoir shutdown Mt. Diablo. SCU has engulfed Henry W. Coe State Park near Morgan Hill, Joseph D. Grant County Park and Blue Oak Ranch Reserve approaching San Jose, while Mission Peak, the Sunol Regional Wilderness, Ohlone Wilderness, and Calaveras Reservoir have been impacted by flames. Although most of the SCU Photo courtesy of California State Parks California State Parks have announced several closures. area has been open space, the fire is rapidly approaching Patterson in Stanislaus County, with an estimated population of 22,524 and has caused destruction in the nearby Diablo Grande community. In Fremont near Mission Peak, residents along Mission Boulevard have received evacuation warnings. Residents south of Livermore and Pleasanton have also been warned. The SCU fire, only 15 percent contained, has destroyed 18 structures and damaged another six, while injuring five individuals. In the CZU zones, fires in Santa Cruz and San Mateo counties have resulted in approximately 77,000 evacuations as of Tuesday. The CZU has closed all San Mateo County parks and State Beaches. It’s destroyed 330 structures and damaged 32 with just 17 percent containment, notably overtaking the historic Big Basin Headquarters and nature center. The State Park is the oldest in California, established in 1902 to preserve some of the state’s oldest stand of old-growth redwoods. The park’s headquarters’ walls were erected in 1932. (See story on page 15 for more information) In Pescadero, the historic Pie Ranch farmhouse – built in 1863 – was destroyed after an ember fell onto their grounds. The mountain town of Boulder Creek is in the midst of a firefight, causing the destruction of 100 homes. A death was recorded in Davenport. Although the SCU and CZU fires are nearest to the Bay, the LNU has been the most destructive with nearly 1,000 structures destroyed along with four injuries and five deaths. articles.text: The JV football team has room for more players. Staff Photo Varsity football coach Jerome Johnson (right) plans a virtual program via Zoom for the JV team, similar to what they used during the summer. JV head coach Daniel King, and assistant Scott Kail are eager to implement a virtual program similar to college and the pros. “Daniel, Scott, and I would like to put kids in our virtual program and show them that football is not all physical – show them the nuances of the game,” said Johnson. “High football IQ goes such a long way. You may not be the fastest, strongest, or biggest, but if you know how to plan for an opponent, study concepts, take angles correctly, it pays such larger dividends,” he said. Through Zoom technology, student athletes are getting acclimated to football in the classroom setting, building their IQ of the game. The goal: put the brains to brawn and see what translates onto the field. “We can really go step-bystep. Kids are engaged, ask a lot of questions and we can go over teaching the game of football. Now the teachable moments are unique since we’re in a classroom setting. Usually when we have a lot of open space, kids are more engaged with each other as compared to with the coaches in this virtual setting,” said Johnson. The JV program currently has around 20 players, and it is eager to find more young talent. Although there will be some expected holdovers from the previous team, the Scots have perpetually been the pipeline for many instant starters. “We would like to add 10-15 more players. We’re going to keep kids engaged and make sure we’re having our program improve while doing it safely,” said Johnson. Despite last year’s Scots winning just one game last fall, the 2018 team was undefeated in its 10-game schedule. It included RB Brian Cain, DB/WR Ben Marshburn, CB/WR Alex Hilton, QB/ WR Tommy McNeal, and QB Cal Barna. Staff Photo Varsity football coach Jerome Johnson (right) plans a virtual program via Zoom for the JV team, similar to what they used during the summer. JV head coach Daniel King, and assistant Scott Kail are eager to implement a virtual program similar to college and the pros. “Daniel, Scott, and I would like to put kids in our virtual program and show them that football is not all physical – show them the nuances of the game,” said Johnson. “High football IQ goes such a long way. You may not be the fastest, strongest, or biggest, but if you know how to plan for an opponent, study concepts, take angles correctly, it pays such larger dividends,” he said. Through Zoom technology, student athletes are getting acclimated to football in the classroom setting, building their IQ of the game. The goal: put the brains to brawn and see what translates onto the field. “We can really go step-bystep. Kids are engaged, ask a lot of questions and we can go over teaching the game of football. Now the teachable moments are unique since we’re in a classroom setting. Usually when we have a lot of open space, kids are more engaged with each other as compared to with the coaches in this virtual setting,” said Johnson. The JV program currently has around 20 players, and it is eager to find more young talent. Although there will be some expected holdovers from the previous team, the Scots have perpetually been the pipeline for many instant starters. “We would like to add 10-15 more players. We’re going to keep kids engaged and make sure we’re having our program improve while doing it safely,” said Johnson. Despite last year’s Scots winning just one game last fall, the 2018 team was undefeated in its 10-game schedule. It included RB Brian Cain, DB/WR Ben Marshburn, CB/WR Alex Hilton, QB/ WR Tommy McNeal, and QB Cal Barna. Former JV players from 2019, such as running back Nico Defazio were praised by OL coach Dick Carte, who mentioned that Evan McConathy and Lucas Bernales will likely have larger roles on the varsity this coming season. articles.text: Photo courtesy of Time Magazine The charred remains of the Big Basin Redwoods State Park headquarters. Last week on Thursday, August 20, park officials announced that the CZU Fire waging in San Mateo County and the Santa Cruz Mountains have destroyed Big Basin Redwood State Park’s historic headquarters, visitor’s center, and campgrounds. The headquarters building was created as a WPA project and is made of stone and redwood logs. It served as park headquarters until its destruction by fire this week. “The historic structures in California’s first state park are almost completely destroyed. It’s awful,” said Save the Redwoods League President Sam Hodder. “We are grateful that everybody got out and everybody is safe. “To have lost something that has been transforming people’s lives for years, such an iconic place, such a terrific example of what parks mean to communities, it’s heartbreaking.” Big Basin is the oldest state park in California, dating back to 1902, and contains some redwood tees believed to be 2,000 years old. The park protects 35,000 acres of redwoods in the Santa Cruz Mountains, including approximately 10,800 acres of oldgrowth Redwoods. As of Tuesday, the Associated Press confirmed that “most” of the park’s old-growth redwoods had survived the burn. Among them, the “Mother of the Forest,” a tree with a 70-foot circumference and height of 329 feet – the equivalent of a 33-story building. Santa Cruz park superintendent Chris Spohrer indicated that damage to trees was widespread and that much of the canopy had been scorched. “From what they described, it was a high-heat, high-intensity fire,” Spohrer said. “A lot of the canopy burned. It is too early to tell what the long-term damage is Photo courtesy of Time Magazine The original Big Basin headquarters building. Photo courtesy of Time Magazine Photo courtesy of the Santa Cruz Sentinel A down redwood tree in Big Basin. Another angle of the Big Basin Headquarters. going to be to those trees.” Although stretches of redwoods will lose their canopies, Save the Redwoods’ scientist and ecologist Kristen Shive mentioned that burn marks will be visible for a while, but the resilience of Redwood trees will help “eventually recover.” “An active crown fire could kill trees,” said Shive. “In many cases, they will look sickly and sad for a while, but they can eventually recover.” Regarding misleading reports of the State Park being totally destroyed, Sempervirens Fund conservationist Laura McLendon agreed that redwoods will recover from the fire and make them stronger. “The forest is not gone,” McLendon said. “It will regrow. Every old growth redwood I’ve ever seen, in Big Basin and other parks, has fire scars on them. They’ve been through multiple fires, possibly worse than this.” As of Tuesday morning, the CZU Lightning Complex fire had burned 78,869-acres and was 17 percent contained. pages.text: 16 Wednesday, August 26, 2020 Back to School By Beatriz Martinez When shelter in place began, a lot of us in Piedmont had to quickly adapt study and work areas in our home. It was then that I realized that no-one in our home had the right set up to be eight hours sitting in front of a computer. My daughter did her homework on the floor or on her bed, my home office wasn’t ready for daily zoom calls or privacy, my living room became my zoom meditation studio, and my son converted our garage into a teen lounge room. Once it was clear that we had entered a new way of home living, it made me rethink my entire home-live-work flow. I had to quickly find effective solutions in creating homeschool spaces for my kids. As a designer I love learning about a problem and finding functional solutions while creating a beautiful environment. So, my business partner and I got on the task and created a list of design components that will help parents the way it helps us when we are designing. 1. LIGHTING – Natural & Artificial Natural lighting is proven to help improve focus, alertness, productivity, and happiness. Adequate artificial lighting helps improve mood and energy, while poor lighting contributes to depression and deficiencies in the body. articles.text: As the Head of a school, I deliver a pretty standard Backto-School message under normal circumstances. You all know the drill: a fresh start, the smell of new pencils, setting goals. Blah, blah, blah. In fact, if you’re like most parents, you probably don’t really listen to these messages because they’re often predictable and dull. I don’t blame you. But these are not normal circumstances. This year, as the school year begins, I am called to address a situation so alarming and unprecedented that I am truly at a loss for words. There’s literally nothing I can say that can put this crisis into perspective, given that perspective is the exact thing you don’t have in the middle of a crisis. I also can’t offer much hope by, say, predicting when we’re going to get a vaccine and return to school full time. I can’t even say for sure which risks are worth taking and which ones aren’t Education is important Commit to supporting each other through the pandemic. because every family is different. So, as the school year begins, I am speechless, or more accurately, I have nothing of consequence to say. Except, maybe, for this. What has buoyed me these past few months, as I plan for the opening of school, are the strikingly honest conversations I’ve had with parents who have contacted me to share their concerns. What Covid has done is stripped away the need for the social niceties that often get in the way of the truth. As a result, every conversation I’ve had has been meaningful, sometimes poignant, and often soulful. People are speaking from the heart, and sometimes their hearts are breaking, and this is sacred ground. The war against this virus, and all of its attendant complications, has many fronts, and it doesn’t need one more. Let’s make it our goal not to wage a battle against each other as school begins. No one has a clear answer about how to navigate this uncharted territory, therefore we can all learn something from each other. And more than that. We can support each other on this journey because, the truth is, all of our hearts are breaking. Dr. Susan Eva Porter is the Head of School at Orinda Academy, an intentionally small independent high school that supports students who think and learn differently. She can be reached at sue@orindaacademy.org.

articles.text: West Edge Opera has announced the launch of “Aperture,” an online platform to create a new opera and music theater in a world where artists are separated from their audiences. The announcement follows the postponement of the Opera’s 2020 season. West Edge Opera is taking the time to invent a program that brings the creative process of new opera directly to the people who are most invested in the art form. “Aperture” seeks to redefine the way operas are chosen for commission and will provide opportunities for both experienced composers and librettist teams, as well as new talent from diverse backgrounds. Select teams will receive commissions of $60,000 and a live performance of the work when it is safe to gather again. Subscribing members of the new program will receive twiceweekly emails filled with video progress reports, analysis, and mini documentaries that discuss the work being made, as well as candid glimpses into the featured artists’ lives. West Edge Opera General Director Mark Streshinksy says he found inspiration for the program in his daily rituals. “The pandemic has been really hard for everyone in the performing arts,” he said. “For me, some days it felt like [actor] Leslie Jordan’s little 90-second updates on Instgram were the highlights of my day. I thought, what if we could do that for new opera? West Edge has found such success with Snapshot [a new work series]. I thought maybe an online version could keep people connected and creating,” he said. “As a composer without much hope of in-person performance any time soon, I found myself without much incentive to write,” said Snapshot co-creator Brian Rosen. “A program like this could bring creators closer to the people who care that these works are still being made. That sort of interaction could keep creativity going Photo by Mark Mayfield West Edge Opera General Director Mark Streshinksy. while we’re trapped in our home.” Aperture will be open for submissions in late August and selected artistic teams will start to be notified in late September. General Membership will be open to the public in late October and will range from $15 to $90 per month, with more access and interactivity offered at higher levels of membership. articles.text: The Piedmont Fire Department will host a screening of the award-winning documentary Wilder than Wild: Fire, Forests and the Future on Monday, August 31, at 6 p.m. It will be shown on the city’s television station, KCOM, Channel 27, to be followed by a panel discussion on wildfire preparation and disaster preparedness. Wilder than Wild, the 2018 documentary written, directed a produced by Emmy Award winners Kevin White and Stephen Most, is a one-hour documentary that reveals how fuel build-up and climate change have exposed Western wild lands to large, high intensity wildfires, while greenhouse gases released from these fires contribute to global warming. The film explores strategies that are being developed to help mitigate the impact of these fires. Ken Pimlott, Director of California Department of Forestry and Fire Protection (Cal Fire), described the documentary as “an absolutely wonderful production. The messages in this film are spot on.” A panel featuring the director and producer Kevin White, and Piedmont Fire Chief Bret Black will follow the screening. “The city of Piedmont wants to build community awareness about mitigation strategies in this new age of wildfire,” Black said. “The screening is part of a larger effort by the city to engage the community in conversations about the future of wildfire, specifically in an urban setting.” Residents can view the screening by tuning in to KCOM or AT&T channel 99. Residents can also watch Wilder than Wild on the Zoom platform by clicking the following link: https://us02web. zoom.us/j/84429317342. For additional information, contact Bret Black at bblack@ piedmont.ca.gov.

articles.text: Lafayette-based Gold Coast Chamber Players has announced plans for two new series of virtual concerts: Bach Shorts and Main Stage Concerts. The first series, Bach Shorts, consists of three one-hour, livestreamed performances that seek to connect us through an intimate exploration of Bach’s Cello Suites. Three leading Bay Area cellists partner with professors, composers, and musicians from around the globe for uniquely personal performances and collaborations. The series begins on Sunday, September 13 at 4 p.m. with cellist Christopher Costanza, from the St. Lawrence String Quartet. He will perform Bach’s Second and Sixth Cello Suites and will partner with Stanford Professor Jonathan Berger, who will discuss the effect music has on the brain, hence the concert title, Bach and the Dancing Brain. On October 11, GCCP presents Bach Inspired, a concert featuring Jennifer Kloetzel, former cellist with the Cypress Quartet. She will perform Bach’s popular First Cello Suite, paired with a world premiere by composer Elena Ruehr called Cricket the Fiddler. Elena will be on hand to share how Bach’s First Suite inspired her composition. The Bach Shorts series concludes on Sunday, November 8 with Bach Connections, with cellist Robert Howard from American Bach Soloists and Philharmonia Baroque Orchestra. He will perform Bach’s Fourth Cello Suite and explore Bach’s universal appeal as he collaborates with cellists from Kenya and Colombia. More Music Next Year After the New Year, Gold Coast Chamber Players plan to offer four live-streamed Main Stage performances with a feeling similar to what Gold Coast audiences have come to enjoy. articles.text: Jude Law as conspiracy theorist Alan Krumwiede in Contagion. Movie review by Chris Honoré Consider the still memorable template: The year is 1918, World War I is underway, and for almost two years a pandemic, also known as the Spanish Flu, grips the world. It’s origin is still unknown, its impact staggering. Some 500 million people were infected and an estimated 50,000,000 to 100,000,000 people died. Panic swept the globe, white masks were ubiquitous, required in all public places, the signature image of a virus that no one was equipped to deal with. But that was then and this is now. Or, more accurately, this is Hollywood where all of life’s events and vagaries offer material for screenwriters, especially a harrowing epidemic and all its contemporary possibilities. Recall Outbreak, released some years back. In the film’s setup we see an infected person sneezing in a movie theater. It was a hold-your-breath moment as the small particles went aerosol. Contagion has countless such moments, small and large. The film opens with a dark screen and the sound of a dry, hacking cough. articles.text: A scene from Howl’s Moving Castle. Review by Chris Honoré Howl’s Moving Castle represents another tour de force from the extraordinary imagination of writer-director Hayao Miyazaki and his world-renowned Studio Ghibli. Adapted from the novel by Diana Wynne Jones, it is set in Europe and features an 18-year-old girl, Sophie (Emily Mortimer), a shy young hat maker, who is transformed into a 90-year-old woman (Jean Simmons) by the jealous Wicked Witch of the Waste (Lauren Bacall), a sly name reflecting Miyazaki’s wonderful sense of humor. Looking in the mirror Sophie is shocked to see a stooped and gnarled old woman and it becomes her quest to somehow break the Witch’s spell. Unexpectedly she meets an attractive, inscrutable, shape-shifting Wizard, Howl (Christian Bale), who lives in a mobile, steampunkish, labyrinthine four-legged castle. This is a Miyazaki tale and Sophie’s adventure soon veers off in unexpected directions, involving a war, a fire demon (Billy Crystal), and even a silent, sentient scarecrow. As well, unlike many of Hollywood’s films aimed at a younger audience, Miyazaki does not draw deep lines between good and evil, often seeming more comfortable with the ambiguous. For example, the Wizard can seem both malicious and benign; Sophie comes to care for the Witch who cast the transformative spell. With regards to war, it’s never clear what side should prevail. The story also seems to ask the question whether war is not only futile but also an absurd human endeavor. All of the above is framed by understated humor and a sense of floating animé, which is vibrant, engaging, and filled with wonder. Note: Howl’s Moving Castle may be too intense for very young children, In addition, its plot is a bit convoluted, taking many different twists and turns. Howl’s Moving Castle (2004). Written and directed by Hayao Miyazaki. From Studio Ghibli and HBO Max. Animated, with the voices of Emily Mortimer, Billy Crystal, Jean Simmons, Lauren Bacall and Christian Bale. 2 hrs. Rated: PG.

articles.text: Review by Chris Honoré Films such as The Karate Kid are, unabashedly, morality plays. The field of play is the context of choice given that sports are so ideally suited to this predictable yet compelling narrative. Adversity is confronted and overcome, the athlete prevails, then smash cut to cheers, raised arms. Get ready for a warm glow. The wildly popular 80s martial arts classic of the same name, starring Pat Morita and Ralph Macchio, was set in Los Angeles. The more recent incarnation takes place, interestingly enough, in Beijing and the sport is not karate but kung fu. Actually, it’s wushu, a more aggressive form of kung fu, involving punching and hard body contact. The template is familiar and the changes regarding geography and culture, when it comes to the core story, superficial. A young kid, Dre (Jaden Smith), from the streets of Detroit, arrives in China with his single mom, Sherry (Taraji P. Henson), who has a job with a car company. Dre is the new kid on the unfamiliar block and soon becomes the target of some local school bullies who are schooled by a cruel sensei in the art of kung fu. Dre’s life quickly becomes intolerable until he is rescued, literally, by the unassuming Mr. Han (Jackie Chan), the apartment building maintenance man, a man generally laconic yet deeply schooled in the martial arts, which he quickly makes obvious when Dre is attacked. Of course, there is a tween love interest, Mei Ying (Wen Wen Han), a gifted violinist, who befriends Dre. And so, Dre’s training begins, including the familiar wax on, wax off, only involving a jacket. Jacket on, hang up, jacket off. Rinse and repeat. Dre is undisciplined and angry; he wants to go home and feels like a stranger in a strange land. He is, nevertheless, quietly and firmly instructed in the lessons of Kung Fu and in the lessons of life, all leading to the familiar climactic match where he meets his nemesis, Cheng, on the mat. The ending is foregone, the building tide of good feelings and anticipation are finalized with Dre performing a slo-mo kicking somersault that is the money moment in the film. Take note: Jaden Smith is the son of actor Will Smith and his wife, Jada Pinkett Smith, who were the film’s producers. His debut acting role was with his father in The Pursuit of Happyness. It must be nice to have a mom and dad who can gift wrap a movie and let you carry it on your pre-teen shoulders. Of course, Jackie Chan’s crew helped with Jaden’s intense training and execution. Tweens will love the story, for them fresh and interesting as well as a nice introduction to China. To the filmmakers’ credit, the neighborhoods of Beijing are not scrubbed, but nicely frayed and crowded giving a solid sense of the bustling and crowded Beijing. It feels like the real deal. And so, once again, does the movie. The Karate Kid. A remake starring Jaden Smith, Jackie Chan, Taraji P. Henson, Wang Zhenwei and Wen wen Han. Directed by Harald Swart. 2 hrs., 20 min.

articles.text: The COVID-19 pandemic has unsettled the country’s employment picture for months and will likely continue to do so for a while. However, the nature and terminology of this disruption varies greatly among individuals – some have seen their jobs disappear, others have been “furloughed” and still others have been offered an early retirement. If you’re in this final group – those either offered, or feeling forced to accept, an early retirement, how should you respond? Try to look at your situation holistically, rather than strictly in a short-term manner. Consider these four areas: • RETIREMENT What does retirement really look like to you? Are you ready to fully retire or would you like to work part time? Are you confident that you can work somewhere else for a few years before retiring on your own terms? If you’re not certain you can work elsewhere, how can you adjust your desired retirement lifestyle – what you planned to do, where you hoped to live, etc. – to meet your new reality? • INCOME Just how financially affected you’ll be from an early retirement depends on several factors: how much you’ve already saved and invested, whether you’re married and have a working spouse, whether you’ve paid off your mortgage, and so on. In any case, though, you’ll need to answer several questions, including these: Do I need to start taking withdrawals from my IRA and 401(k)? If so, how much can I afford to take out each year without running the risk of outliving my resources? Should I adjust my current investment mix? If I haven’t yet started collecting Social Security, should I do so now, or can I afford to wait until my monthly payments will be bigger? Are there any other sources of income I can leverage? You may want to work with a financial professional to address these and other key income-related issues. • INSURANCE If you received health insurance through your employer, an early retirement could present you with a dilemma, especially if you’re not quite old enough for Medicare. You might be eligible for COBRA, which provides ex-employees and their dependents the option of continued health insurance for potentially up to 36 months, but this coverage can be expensive. As an alternative, you might be able to negotiate an extended severance package, which could provide you with health insurance for several months. Or, you might be able to get on the health insurance plan of your working spouse. • LEGACY Many people want to take care of their family while they’re alive – and leave something behind when they’re gone. If you take an early retirement, you might lose your employer’s group life insurance. Of course, if this plan was not sufficient, you may have already supplemented it with your own policy, but, if you haven’t, you may need to shop around for some coverage, particularly if you have children still at home. You also may want to take this opportunity to review your key financial accounts to make sure your beneficiary designations still accurately reflect your wishes. Going through an unplanned career transition is certainly challenging. But looking closely at the four areas describe above, and making the appropriate moves, may help you reduce some of the stress and can put you in a better position to start the next phase of your life. If so, how much can I afford to take out each year without running the risk of outliving my resources? Should I adjust my current investment mix? If I haven’t yet started collecting Social Security, should I do so now, or can I afford to wait until my monthly payments will be bigger? Are there any other sources of income I can leverage? You may want to work with a financial professional to address these and other key income-related issues. • INSURANCE If you received health insurance through your employer, an early retirement could present you with a dilemma, especially if you’re not quite old enough for Medicare. You might be eligible for COBRA, which provides ex-employees and their dependents the option of continued health insurance for potentially up to 36 months, but this coverage can be expensive. As an alternative, you might be able to negotiate an extended severance package, which could provide you with health insurance for several months. Or, you might be able to get on the health insurance plan of your working spouse. • LEGACY Many people want to take care of their family while they’re alive – and leave something behind when they’re gone. If you take an early retirement, you might lose your employer’s group life insurance. Of course, if this plan was not sufficient, you may have already supplemented it with your own policy, but, if you haven’t, you may need to shop around for some coverage, particularly if you have children still at home. You also may want to take this opportunity to review your key financial accounts to make sure your beneficiary designations still accurately reflect your wishes. Going through an unplanned career transition is certainly challenging. But looking closely at the four areas describe above, and making the appropriate moves, may help you reduce some of the stress and can put you in a better position to start the next phase of your life. articles.text: The Piedmont Recreation Department’s First Mondays Reading Group took on one of its more challenging reads for its monthly discussion on Monday, August 3, when it tackled The Black Swan: The Impact of the Highly Improbable, by author and former options trader Nassim Nicholas Taleb. Written in 2007 and updated in 2010, the book provides an understanding of rare and unpredictable events, their extreme impacts, and the tendency for people to find simplistic explanations for these events after they have happened. Taleb calls them “Black Swans”, using 9/11 is an example. The book was on the New York Times best-seller list for 36 weeks and was published in 32 languages. Taleb explains there are different types of events and probabilities associated with them. We cannot anticipate the black swans that dramatically affect us. Taleb does not suggest attempting to predict Black Swan events, but rather wants readers to develop the capacity to handle them and have the ability to take advantage of them when they unexpectedly occur. His central thesis is that we have a blindness with respect to randomness, particularly those with large deviations; and the consequences for us are profound. Taleb is a philosopher, mathematician, psychologist, social scientist, and financial trader, all wrapped up in one very intelligent man. He covers literary topics, psychology, science, business, and advises his readers on how to conduct themselves in the face of uncertainty. Following his thoughts requires focus and effort from the reader, but the group of thirteen readers was up to the challenge. Participating in the virtual meeting were Sarah Johnson, Nancy Henn, Mike Henn, Melba Yee, Susan Ode, Jeri Lockhart, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Albert Chen, Sally Arney, Margie Blodgett, Dick Carter, and group leaders Priscilla Wanerus and Carol Long. Most members of the group were happy to have read the book. They felt it will affect the way they will perceive and react to the uncertainties they experience. It was worth reading, but not the type of book that many of them usually read. Some readers felt that reading the book was like going back to school for better or worse. Others had issues with the book and the author’s style. Some found Taleb’s writing imperfect. There is humor, but sometimes Taleb takes what the readers felt were snarky shots at people with whom he disagrees. Taleb seems to have particular issues with the French, which might in part be explained by his Lebanese ancestry. Reading The Black Swan may be somewhat like going through boot camp – it is hard. Not all the experiences are enjoyable, but you are better off from doing it. Reading this book is another example of the benefits of a participating in the First Mondays Reading Group. It asks its members to read good books that they might not otherwise read. Ultimately, they enjoy and benefit from the mental stretching this requires. With their book discussion complete, the group discussed what to read next. However, during July some concerns with White Fragility had been expressed. With the recent death of Civil Rights leader, Congressman John Lewis, and our society’s current focus on racial justice, the group decided to replace White Fragility with Across That Bridge, a book by Rep. Lewis, for their September read. The group will read The Dutch House for an October discussion. Assuming social distancing is still in place, the readers will meet again in a September Zoom call. articles.text: Observations of the built environment of a beautiful city The landscaping, the streets, the buildings and the resulting neighborhoods are in some cases nice, in many cases outstanding, and sometimes incredible! My focus is walking with the purpose of soaking in the design of the city and then reflecting on why it is the beautiful place it is—and what makes it this way? My daily excursions of the last months have led to a number of observations, thoughts, and a few conclusions on the built environment of Piedmont, which I would like to share with people. But first a word on walking itself. There is an old Steve Martin movie, LA Story, where, needing to visit his next door neighbor, he walks out the front of his house, gets in his car, and drives the 60 feet or so to his neighbor’s house. This scene is funny, but also of course a statement on our car-dependent culture, ramifications of which spread to all parts of the places in which we live. Simply walking mitigates this dependency and many of its related side effects. Not only does going on foot have obvious health benefits, but it adds zero traffic and pollution to our lives. Further, it facilitates meeting and talking to other people, to neighbors—it facilitates community. Although not always possible for some people because of physical limitations or geographical difficulties, going on foot is also, and perhaps most importantly, the best way to truly see, reflect on, and appreciate a neighborhood, a building or a place. The built-in slow pace of walking can’t be duplicated on a bicycle, and certainly not in a car. When I am walking and looking, the main questions I always have is: Is this nice? Is this beautiful? Or, is this lacking? Is this bad? And then, why? The answers are sometimes easy and obvious, but sometimes not. A viable evaluation depends on reflection and an understanding of the different components and design principles involved. And like a work of art, there are intangibles that are a result of, but transcend all the pieces. Because we are all so greatly affected by the built environment in which we live, I believe we all can benefit from this kind of discussion. In this column over the next number of weeks I will be focusing on various of my design observations from walking through Piedmont, including those related to the urban design, the landscaping architecture, and of course, the architecture. I encourage others to do the same, looking, evaluating and forming their own opinions as well. Wouldn’t it be better to pop the bags in someone’s garbage can? Piedmont Poop Alert. Max the mix puppy and Amelia Dear Abby: It seems that many of the animal adoption centers do not have puppies. We need a smallish dog to bring us a smile while we work from home. It’s the perfect time for us to train a puppy, but we’re striking out. Any suggestions who might have a lucky puppy? Perplexed, Toni and Amy Dear Max and Amelia: Here are three possibilities. 1. Used poop bags are typically left by dog owners (near sidewalks) with the idea that they’ll pick them up on the way back home. Sometimes routes are changed and the bags are left and forgotten. 2. Some dog walkers drop the bags with the understanding that other dog walkers will pick them up and drop them in a public waste can. However, they might be picked up but they might not. 3. The idea of dropping a poop bag in someone’s garbage is complicated. Would I mind if you did that in our cans? Some non-dog owners say absolutely not. They don’t want the bags slipped into their garbage— the smell is not welcome. So it’s best to hang onto those bags and drop them in the public waste or when you return home. That’s the scoop on the poop, –Abby Dear Toni and Amy: There is a wonderful organization called Dog is My Co-Pilot that brings dogs and cats from Texas which seems to have a lot of adoptees to the western states, which are running out of dogs of all sizes to adopt. Dr. Peter Rork, a retired orthopedic surgeon, flies his own plane to Houston every two weeks and brings dogs of all ages to Merced, Portland, Salt Lake City, and other locations. Dr. Rork says he brings back mostly dogs on his trips, as many as 200, but also a few kittens too. In total, he thinks he’s helped place over 15,000 animals in adoption, one tail at a time. articles.text: Map asserts southeastern part of Piedmont is part of zone, which may expand in the future The City will officially adopt a map as part of its City Code that asserts a portion of southeastern Piedmont is part of a Very High Fire Severity Zone on Wednesday, September 16. The map detailing the zone was set by CalFire several decades ago in the wake of the Oakland Hills Fire in 1991. State law gives local cities the option to work with CalFire authorities to adopt fire prevention ordinances revolving areas that are at a higher fire risk. These ordinances require properties in these high-risk zones to maintain fire defense improvements. In 2019, all cities were required to adopt CalFire’s Very High Fire Severity Zone map by ordinance. The map was last updated in 2008, and state authorities are pushing to update it but have been delayed due to the coronavirus pandemic. Piedmont Fire Chief Bret Black said that when the map is updated, new methodologies will be used and it is likely that the Very High Fire Severity Zone in Piedmont will expand. Right now, the Very High Fire Severity Zone includes most of the area between La Salle Avenue to Park Boulevard, although a few neighborhoods are exempt. It also includes the area surrounding Tyson Lake. This amounts to roughly 20 percent of the City. The zone is part of wider designation that runs through the Oakland Hills. All of Piedmont is part of a state-designated Wildland Urban Interface Fire Area. “Piedmont’s unique topography and geography make the entire City particularly susceptible to fires,” the ordinance, which had a second reading unanimously approved by City Council on Monday, August 17, states. All of the City must follow state vegetation maintenance standards, with homeowners living the Very High Fire Severity Zone following stricter standards. These standards require residents to cut down and remove hazardous vegetation, like dead trees or brush, from the property. There must be a 30-foot perimeter around each structure that is a “defensible space,” meaning an area where wildfire prevention practices are in place. Roadways must be kept clear of vegetation. Additionally, roofs and gutters need to be regularly cleaned and maintained. The full standards can found in the City Code. Black told the Post that the Piedmont Fire Department has been applying California’s vegetation management standards in the Very High Fire Severity Zone and around the rest of the City for years, but now Piedmont has adopted the official state map. PFD has been conducting inspections of properties for fire risk since the 1990s. He noted that all Piedmont residents are required to maintain defensible space, officially defined as “the area adjacent to a structure or dwelling where wildfire prevention or protection practices are implemented to provide defense from an approaching wildfire or to minimize the spread of a structure fire to wildlands or surrounding areas,” regardless of if they live in the Very High Fire Severity Zone. “We are making our Code match our practices,” Black commented. In the ordinance, PFD indicated several plants and trees that are considered flammable vegetation, including California Bay, Cedar, Cypress, Eucalyptus, Fir, Palm, Pine, Manzanita and Pampas grass. These plants are not prohibited, but are known by the state have a high resin or sap content and, therefore, are more flammable. PFD will require the removal of dead trees or other vegetation, regardless of species. “Any dead, dying, or unhealthy vegetation will be required to be addressed whether or not the species is listed,” Black said. In a staff report, Black explained that these requirements are written in a way to allow PFD discretion with how they are enforced, so as to be reasonable in their implementation. The goal was to make these requirements achievable for homeowners but also ensuring that wildfire hazards are as mitigated as possible. The City noted that as PFD increases the number of inspections, especially in light of a dangerous 2020 wildfire season already underway, “residents may initially see an increase in costs to comply with these proposed standards.” However, the City noted that ongoing compliance costs should be in line with current landscape maintenance costs. articles.text: On Friday, August 21, the Alameda County Public Health Office issued a revised shelter-inplace order, effective this Friday, August 28. The revised order allows the reopening of pools, permission for outdoor personal care services, and permission for outdoor tasting at wineries. Pools may open but with a reduced number of swimmers, and will require appointments. Lane limitations will be utilized to allow for physical distancing. Aquatic fitness classes are allowed with these restrictions. Poolside and deck furniture is not permitted, and lounging by pool areas is still not permitted in the county. Sanitation practices must be observed. All indoor areas associated with the pool, including locker and shower areas, with the exception of restrooms, will remain closed, including common areas, snack bars, lounging and sunbathing areas. This is the first guidance issued by Alameda County for the reopening of pools. The City of Piedmont has said it will spend the next two weeks determining whether the conditions imposed by the order can be applied to reopen the Piedmont Community Pool. City staff developed reopening frameworks based upon guidance from other health jurisdictions in Northern California. “The city understands the importance of the pool to the community and will examine whether reopening under the requirements imposed by the order is practicable. It is likely a decision on whether to reopen the Piedmont Community Pool will be considered by the city council at its meeting of September 8,” wrote City Clerk John Tulloch. Personal Service Providers, a term used by the county and state that includes hair salons, barbershops, nail salons, skin care, waxing, and non-medical massage providers, may provide services outdoors starting August 28. These services are subject to applicable state and local guidance Wineries may now allow patrons to visit outdoor tasting facilities. Previously, wineries were only permitted to serve wine or allow for wine tasting with a meal or food order. The county confirmed that schools must continue distance learning, and not accept waivers for in-person learning at this time. In-person instruction is permitted for children in psychiatric health facilities, or crisis housing units. Extracurricular activities at schools are permitted on school campuses for groups up to 14.
articles.title: Pools, outdoor salons given go-ahead to reopen
